source.title: Multimodal-Guided Dynamic Dataset Pruning for Robust and Efficient Data-Centric Learning
source.authors: Suorong Yang; Peijia Li; Yu-Jie Liu; Zhiming Xu; Peng Ye; Wan-Li Ouyang; Fu-Rao Shen; Dong-Zhan Zhou

record.tranche_reason: Reports held-out accuracy under dynamic dataset pruning, a training-data selection setting not covered by the listed versions; it does not measure the train–test gap.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test accuracy for data-selection methods and ratios. These results do not measure training error or identify whether any change is due to a smaller train–test gap.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates its own dynamic pruning method, not any listed claim version. It cites Feldman and Zhang (2020), but does not identify memorized examples by their inclusion effect or compare removing them with random removal. Held-out accuracy alone is sufficient for several versions; the issue here is the different intervention, not the missing train–test gap.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that dynamic pruning combining task loss and pretrained CLIP semantic consistency reduces redundancy and accelerates training while maintaining or improving performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study prunes training samples dynamically using task-loss and cross-modal consistency scores; it does not use the listed versions' interventions or measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Selection ratio and dataset change the reported accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Dynamic task-loss and CLIP-consistency selection yields CIFAR-10 accuracies of 94.9%, 95.1%, and 95.9% versus 95.6% with full data; CIFAR-100 accuracies are 77.4%, 78.7%, and 78.9% versus 78.2%. ImageNet accuracy is 76.8% at 60% selection versus 76.4% with full data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dynamic pruning using task difficulty and multimodal semantic consistency can maintain or improve held-out accuracy while reducing the samples used per epoch.

record.problems: Training error and train–test gaps are not reported. The text does not state uncertainty estimates for the tabulated accuracies.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 also reports other baseline methods at each selection ratio; those are comparisons among pruning methods, not additional measurements of a listed claim version. Table 2 includes baseline selection methods, but their accuracy is likewise outside the listed versions.

untested.parts: Matched natural-label and fixed-random-label training, training fit, and held-out accuracy.
Width-dependent test error beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and interactions with augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Identifying memorized examples by their inclusion effect and comparing their removal with equal-sized random removal.

record.verdict_notes: Selection changes each epoch; these experiments do not permanently remove a fixed set of memorized examples and retrain. The qualitative noisy-data illustration also does not test V1 or V8. No additional results bearing on the listed versions were found in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization under the same recipe.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers and their tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the train–test gap.
Removing memorized examples as identified by their influence on correct predictions.
